title: Oil Is Near $100. The US Just Proposed a 12.5 Per Cent Tariff on India. NRI Investors Face a Dual Shock.
excerpt: Iran hostilities pushed Brent crude to $97.81 on Wednesday while Trump's trade office proposed new forced-labour tariffs on 60 economies — including India at the higher 12.5 per cent rate. Here is what it means for Indian markets and your portfolio.
body:
Two shocks hit global markets on Wednesday, and both land squarely on India.

Brent crude settled at $97.81 a barrel — up 1.9 per cent on the day and the highest level since late May — after Iranian attacks damaged Kuwait's airport and injured dozens, while the US military struck a communications tower on the Iranian island of Qeshm near the Strait of Hormuz. Diplomacy to halt the war showed little progress. West Texas Intermediate rose 2.4 per cent to $96.02. Analysts at Mizuho warned that if violence continues to escalate, oil will "trade through $100 sooner rather than later."

Hours earlier, the US Trade Representative's office had dropped a 98-page report proposing new tariffs of up to 12.5 per cent on imports from 60 economies. India was placed among the 45 countries facing the higher rate, accused of failing to impose and effectively enforce a forced-labour import prohibition. The proposal came on the second of three days of trade talks between Indian officials and a US delegation in New Delhi — timing that Delhi is unlikely to view as coincidental.

## Why This Is a Uniquely Indian Problem

India imports over 85 per cent of its crude oil. Every dollar increase in the price of a barrel costs the Indian economy roughly $2.1 billion annually. With Brent approaching the $100 mark, India's import bill is climbing toward levels not seen since the 2022 energy crisis. The rupee, already under pressure from a strong US dollar, weakened further on Wednesday.

For the Indian government, oil above $95 complicates everything. It widens the current account deficit, pushes up petrol and diesel prices at a politically sensitive time, and forces the Reserve Bank of India into an uncomfortable position between supporting growth and defending the currency. India's fiscal deficit target for 2026-27 — set at 4.4 per cent of GDP — becomes harder to hit with every week the Strait of Hormuz remains partially shut.

The tariff proposal adds a second front. The Section 301 investigation, designed to rebuild Trump's emergency tariffs after the Supreme Court struck them down in February, found that India has "failed to impose and effectively enforce a forced labour import prohibition." The proposed 12.5 per cent duty — higher than the 10 per cent facing Canada, the EU, and Mexico — would apply broadly to Indian exports to the United States.

Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative, noted that the finding could be challenged, since the USTR investigation was not about forced labour in Indian exports but whether India blocked imports tied to forced labour elsewhere. But the political signal is clear.

## What It Means for Indian Markets

The Nifty 50 and Sensex, which had been riding a global rally driven by AI euphoria, now face a more hostile backdrop. India's IT services sector — the largest source of US dollar earnings — is largely unaffected by goods tariffs, but Indian pharmaceutical, textile, jewellery, and chemical exports could face significant cost increases if the 12.5 per cent duty takes effect after public hearings on July 7.

The energy sector tells a split story. Oil marketing companies like Indian Oil, BPCL, and HPCL face margin compression if crude stays above $95 and the government resists passing costs to consumers. Upstream producers like ONGC and Oil India benefit from higher realizations but face windfall tax risks.

For NRI investors holding Indian equities or mutual funds, the calculus has shifted. A weaker rupee reduces the dollar value of Indian holdings. Higher oil prices drag on earnings across manufacturing, aviation, and consumer sectors. And the tariff overhang — even if ultimately negotiated down — introduces uncertainty that markets hate.

## The Bigger Picture

What makes this moment different from previous oil shocks or tariff threats is the convergence. India is simultaneously dealing with an energy supply disruption it cannot control, a trade action by its most important partner, and a domestic economy that was just beginning to accelerate after a sluggish first quarter. The combination tests the resilience of a market that has outperformed global peers for two straight years.

The public comment period for the forced-labour tariffs runs through July 6, with hearings starting July 7. Oil markets will be driven by whether the US and Iran can reach even an interim ceasefire. Both timelines suggest the uncertainty will last through the summer.

For NRI investors, the tactical move is to watch the rupee-dollar exchange rate and India's crude oil import bill in June. If Brent sustains above $100 and the tariffs proceed without negotiation, Indian markets could give back some of the gains that made them a global outperformer. If either resolves favourably, the pullback is a buying opportunity.

Neither outcome is clear today. What is clear is that India is more exposed than most to the two biggest macro risks of the moment — and NRI portfolios need to reflect that reality.

*Sources: Reuters; Barron's; Barchart; CNN; LiveMint; Global Trade Research Initiative; US Trade Representative*
